
Tuned for this machine
  llama.cpp build: a build BoltBeam does not know by name, at
  ~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server (CUDA). Its local patches: llama-
  pinned-copy-stream, llama-moe-prefill, llama-server-ckpt-min-head, llama-
  server-ckpt-tail-only.
  Model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-IQ1_M-00001-of-00002.gguf, 48 expert
  layers of 256 experts, 23.42 GiB of experts; 11.07 GiB of them in host RAM
  (--experts-in-ram 24 (given)).
  Host: 31.3 GiB RAM, 28.3 GiB available now, 26 GiB usable for the model;
  L3 32 MiB (sysfs index3: 32 MiB shared by cpus 0-15).
  Read from this machine and the build; nothing ran to get them.

  --cache-ram 0 · derived
    off when the host experts (counted twice when the build can pin them:
    the mmap pages the server still reads and a full pinned copy), the
    tables' resident rows and the default 8 GiB prompt cache exceed the 26
    GiB usable RAM; the pin budget below gets that RAM
  -ub 4096 · derived
    the chunk BoltBeam's prompt limit picks for this machine (the offload
    page's prompt setup): the smallest within the policy tie of the best.
    Measured: host experts are uploaded once per chunk, so bigger chunks
    upload less: with experts in RAM, 4096 measured 15% faster than 2048
    (10k, -ncmoe 12, pinned: 4,312 vs 3,745 tok/s wall)
    to confirm: best over -ub [1024, 2048, 4096, 8192]
  -b 2048 · default
    raised to -ub when -ub is larger (the command does it); a prompt is read
    in chunks of at most -ub, so a -b above -ub adds no larger chunk.
    Measured: with experts in RAM, -b 8192 at -ub 4096 on a 10k prompt
    measured no effect: 4,295 vs 4,312 tok/s (the server's head and near-end
    breaks still set the decode calls)
  LLAMA_WS=1 · default
    on: it only engages for prefill chunks of at least LLAMA_WS_MIN_TOKENS
    tokens with experts in host RAM; decode takes the stock path. Measured:
    with Flash-Next experts in host RAM, decode was unchanged with it on
    (24.6 vs 24.8 tok/s)
  LLAMA_WS_MIN_TOKENS=1024 · default
    left at the patch's 1024: it decides only chunks smaller than it, so it
    matters only with a small -ub. Measured: with Flash-Next experts in host
    RAM, at -ub 4096 on a 10k prompt 256 and 1024 read the same (4,329 vs
    4,312 tok/s wall; the chat head batch is shorter than either); at -ub
    256 and 512 the streamed path read 1.8-1.9x the stock one
  LLAMA_WS_PIN_GIB=12 · derived
    a pinned copy is a second copy: the server's short chunks still read
    every host expert from the mmap, so all 11.07 GiB stay in the page
    cache. Pinned + host experts + tables' resident rows (0.08 GiB) + prompt
    cache (0 GiB) must fit the 26 GiB usable RAM (28.3 GiB available when
    this ran, less the 2 GiB margin). The margin makes it conservative. Run
    it with no other model server holding RAM. What it pins is whole expert
    tensors in load order, not experts by use: a routing profile (boltbeam
    routing MODEL --engine E; on this model the hottest 10% of experts take
    47% of selections) says which experts a pin should hold first, which
    this patch cannot do yet, so that is advice only, not a setting.
    Measured: on the 31 GB box with Flash-Next, -ncmoe 12/18/24 pinned in
    full read best (1.58-1.91x stock); with every expert in RAM (-cmoe) the
    rule allows 1 GiB where 4 GiB read best (+5% over none) and 8 GiB
    collapsed
  GGML_CUDA_WS_RING_MIB=8 · derived
    a quarter of the 32 MiB L3 the copying core shares (sysfs index3: 32 MiB
    shared by cpus 0-15), a power of two: the memcpy's writes stay in cache
    and the DMA reads them from there, so staging is not DRAM-bound twice.
    The quarter comes from one L3 size; on any other it is derived, not
    measured. Measured: on a 32 MiB L3 the quarter (8 MiB as 1 MiB x 8) read
    1,661 tok/s, against 1,563 at 2 MiB, 1,463-1,485 at 16 MiB and 612 at
    512 MiB
  GGML_CUDA_WS_CHUNK_KIB=1024 · derived
    the ring in eight chunks, so the CPU fills one while the DMA drains the
    others; the count of eight comes from one L3 size, and on any other it
    is derived, not measured. Measured: on a 32 MiB L3, 1 MiB x 8 read 1,661
    tok/s against 4 MiB x 4 at 1,463 and 512 KiB x 4 at 1,563
  GGML_CUDA_WS_SLOTS=17 · derived
    derived, not measured: as many slots as hiding the copy needs, but no
    more than fit beside the loaded model. Copy: the largest host expert
    tensor (225 MiB) takes 8.3 ms at this machine's 28.3 GB/s pinned copy
    rate (host scan). Compute: 2.6 ms per layer per 4096-token chunk (the
    prompt limit's GPU time, a lower bound), 0.88 ms per host tensor. So 10
    slots keep each copy ahead of its layer. The copy falls behind compute
    across the 72 host tensors, so 64 of the next chunk's first ones would
    have to be on the card before it starts, but only 7 can be copied while
    the card's own layers finish the chunk before: 17 are useful. Fit: 31.3
    GiB free now, less the model's 16.2 GiB on the card, the KV cache and
    recurrent state (0.34 GiB), an estimated 0.84 GiB compute buffer and the
    1.7 GiB llama-server holds besides (its CUDA context and pools, seen
    once on an RTX 5090), leaves 12.3 GiB after load; less a 1 GiB margin
    that is room for 51 slots. The count is the smaller of the two, at most
    the 72 host expert tensors (more slots have nothing to hold) and never
    below the patch's 4. Too many slots is worse than too few: a slot that
    does not fit fails, and the streamer keeps retrying it. Measured: on an
    RTX 5090 with 12 layers of Flash-Next experts in RAM (-ncmoe 12, 10k
    prompt), 4 slots read 5,415 tok/s wall, 8: 5,495, 12: 5,724, 16: 5,720,
    24: 5,892 (n=6 at 4 and 24, n=2 between), with the copy left exposed at
    chunk starts down from 261.7 to 116.2 ms and outputs bitwise identical;
    32 and 36 slots did not fit beside the loaded model (211 and 203 failed
    slot allocations) and ran slower, 5,062 and 5,231 (n=2). With 18 layers
    in RAM 36 slots fit and screened 5,722 vs 5,523 at 24 (n=2, not
    confirmed). Counts other than these are derived, not measured
    to confirm: start llama-server with the patch's 4 slots, read the GPU
    memory free after load and after one prompt, size the slots from that,
    then run them and back off while the log shows failed slot allocations
  GGML_CUDA_WS_THREADS=1 · default
    the staging copy is bound by RAM, not by one core, so more threads only
    contend for it. Measured: with Flash-Next experts in host RAM, 2 and 4
    threads read slower (880 and 305 vs 1,661 tok/s)
  GGML_CUDA_WS_PAGEABLE=0 · default
    a debugging switch: pageable copies skip the pinned ring the copy stream
    is built around. Measured: with Flash-Next experts in host RAM, pageable
    copies read 751 vs 1,661 tok/s with the ring
  GGML_CUDA_MMID_PAR_MIN=256 · default
    the patch's crossover (outputs are bit-identical either way); --measure
    confirms it on this machine
    to confirm: crossover over -ub [64, 128, 256, 512]
  GGML_CUDA_MMQ_ID_J=(unset) · default
    a sweep knob, left unset: llama.cpp's own mean-columns rule picks the
    tile width
  GGML_CUDA_BATCH_GET_STAGING=1 · default
    on: a reused pinned buffer saves pinning each checkpoint's destination
    afresh, and the results are bit-identical. Measured: with experts in RAM
    (Flash-Next, 10k prompt), each fresh 112 MiB pin cost ~40 ms per
    checkpoint and staging measured +4.5%
  GGML_CUDA_BATCH_GET_STAGING_MAX_MIB=1024 · default
    a cap on pinned memory: a state read larger than it takes the old path.
    Measured: with experts in RAM (Flash-Next), the largest staged span
    measured 448 MiB with the prompt cache on (128 MiB with --cache-ram 0),
    under the cap
  LLAMA_SERVER_CKPT_MIN_HEAD=256 · derived
    ⚠ changes outputs: not bitwise identical
    256 with experts in host RAM: the chat template's short head otherwise
    runs as its own batch, which uploads every host layer's experts from
    pageable memory and then takes a checkpoint sync. Outputs are not
    bitwise identical (the batch boundaries move); checkpoint restore still
    works. Measured: with Flash-Next experts in host RAM the head was 42
    tokens and its batch uploaded 2.6 GB (~250 ms); 256 read +16% at 10k
    (4,551 -> 5,278 tok/s wall) and +53% at 2.7k (3,089 -> 4,731). The first
    argmax divergences were near-ties (top-2 probabilities within 0.01-
    0.09), the same envelope as stock -ub 2048 vs 4096
  LLAMA_SERVER_CKPT_TAIL_ONLY=0 · derived
    off, because the workload is chat (--workload chat, the default): with
    it on, a follow-up that changes an earlier part of the conversation re-
    reads the whole prompt; outputs of a single request are identical. Turn
    it on only for one-shot prompts (--workload one-shot). Measured: on an
    RTX 5090 with 12 layers of Flash-Next experts in RAM (10k chat prompt,
    24 slots, n=6), 5,892 -> 6,016 tok/s wall (+124 tok/s, about 35 ms a
    prompt), against Strata's 6,039 in the same session; the restore test
    lost its restore point (2,215 cached tokens -> 0)

  LLAMA_WS_PIN_GIB=12 GGML_CUDA_WS_SLOTS=17 LLAMA_SERVER_CKPT_MIN_HEAD=256
    ~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server -m /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-
    RCO-IQ1_M-00001-of-00002.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 24 -c 10000 --cache-
    ram 0 -ub 4096 -b 4096
